description: Task evals for the cluster-analysis skill. Each prompt is a realistic clustering decision a practitioner would actually bring. Expectations check for the skill's opinionated, assumption-first reasoning — not just naming an algorithm. A baseline model without the skill tends to name a popular algorithm and hand over boilerplate code; a model with the skill should interrogate assumptions, preprocessing, and validation, and give a defensible recommendation with its catch.

evals.prompt: I've got about 50k points of sensor readings (8 numeric features) and I want to find natural groupings. I don't know how many groups there are, the groups are probably weird shapes, some regions are way denser than others, and there's definitely junk/outlier readings I'd rather not force into a group. I was going to use k-means with the elbow method. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on k-means + elbow for this data and recommends HDBSCAN (density-based, no preset k, variable density, labels noise), with the reasoning tied to the stated data characteristics. Explains why k-means is wrong here (spherical/convex assumption, forces every point into a cluster, needs k) and why plain DBSCAN is worse than HDBSCAN (single global eps can't handle variable density). Mentions scaling the 8 features first and that the elbow method is weak.
expectations: Recommends HDBSCAN as the primary choice
Explains k-means assumes spherical/convex clusters and forces all points into clusters, which mismatches the stated data
Notes that varying density specifically breaks plain DBSCAN's single global eps, motivating HDBSCAN over DBSCAN
Mentions that the data should be scaled/standardized before clustering
Characterizes the elbow method as weak or advisory rather than endorsing it
Notes HDBSCAN labels noise/outliers rather than forcing them into clusters

evals.prompt: What's the right number of clusters for my customer dataset? I ran k-means and the silhouette score is highest at k=6, so I'm going with 6. Just want a sanity check.
evals.expected_output: Validates that silhouette beats the elbow but refuses to bless k=6 on one number. Recommends triangulating multiple criteria (gap statistic, Davies-Bouldin), checking stability via bootstrap/reinitialization, and confirming clusterability (that structure exists at all vs. a null). Notes silhouette assumes convex clusters and that interpretability is a legitimate tiebreaker. Frames the choice of k as under-determined, not a single correct value.
expectations: Does not simply confirm k=6; treats a single index as insufficient justification
Recommends using multiple validation criteria (e.g., gap statistic, Davies-Bouldin, silhouette together)
Recommends a stability check (bootstrap resampling and/or reinitialization)
Raises clusterability / whether real structure exists (e.g., null comparison, Hopkins, or visualization)
States there is no single purely data-driven 'correct' k and/or that interpretability matters

evals.prompt: For my psych study I have ~600 participants and 9 continuous questionnaire subscales. A reviewer suggested latent profile analysis. But I also keep seeing people use Gaussian mixture models and latent class analysis for this kind of thing. Are these different methods? Which should I use and how do I decide the number of profiles?
evals.expected_output: Explains that LPA, GMM, and LCA are the same finite-mixture machinery differing by indicator type and research culture: LPA = Gaussian mixture on continuous indicators (so for 9 continuous subscales, LPA and GMM are the same model), LCA = mixture on categorical indicators. Recommends LPA/GMM here. For choosing profiles, recommends BIC (and ICL/BLRT), reporting entropy/classification certainty, considering class sizes, and using interpretability — not a single statistic. May mention tooling (mclust/tidyLPA/tidySEM/Mplus or sklearn GaussianMixture).
expectations: States that LPA is (a) Gaussian mixture modeling, i.e., LPA and GMM are essentially the same model for continuous indicators
Explains LCA differs by using categorical/binary indicators rather than continuous ones
Recommends LPA (or equivalently a Gaussian mixture) as appropriate for 9 continuous subscales
Recommends BIC for choosing the number of profiles, and mentions at least one of ICL or BLRT
Mentions entropy / classification certainty or interpretability as part of the decision, not just one fit statistic

evals.prompt: My k-means clustering gives garbage results — the clusters don't make any sense and they're dominated by one or two variables. I have features like annual_revenue (millions), employee_count (hundreds to thousands), founding_year, and a satisfaction_score from 1-5. What's going wrong?
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses the cause as preprocessing, specifically unscaled features on wildly different ranges: annual_revenue and employee_count dominate the Euclidean distance, so satisfaction_score (1-5) and founding_year contribute almost nothing. Recommends standardizing/scaling before clustering. May go further: consider whether features are even comparable, whether to log-transform skewed monetary/count variables, and that scaling is a modeling choice. Frames preprocessing as the dominant driver of results.
expectations: Identifies that the features are on vastly different scales and that large-range features (revenue, employee_count) dominate the distance
Recommends scaling/standardizing the features before running k-means
Connects the symptom (clusters dominated by one or two variables) to the unscaled distance metric rather than to k-means itself being wrong
Mentions that preprocessing/distance choices drive clustering results (possibly suggesting log-transforming skewed monetary/count variables)

evals.prompt: I want to segment users for a marketing campaign. My data has both numeric fields (age, total_spend, sessions_per_week) and categorical fields (subscription_tier, acquisition_channel, country). I was going to one-hot encode the categoricals and run k-means on everything. Will that work?
evals.expected_output: Warns that one-hot + k-means on mixed data is problematic: Euclidean distance on one-hot categories imposes arbitrary geometry and high-cardinality fields (like country) inflate dimensionality and dominate distance. Recommends a proper mixed-data approach: Gower distance with k-medoids (PAM), or k-prototypes (with its gamma weight balancing numeric vs categorical). Mentions scaling the numeric part and handling high-cardinality categoricals (e.g., country). May mention LCA only if framed for categorical-only.
expectations: Flags that one-hot encoding categoricals + Euclidean k-means is a poor approach for mixed-type data
Recommends a mixed-data method: Gower distance with k-medoids/PAM, and/or k-prototypes
Notes the problem with high-cardinality categoricals (e.g., country) dominating or exploding the distance/dimensionality
Mentions scaling the numeric features as part of the pipeline

evals.prompt: I read that Affinity Propagation and Mean Shift are great because you don't have to choose the number of clusters. I have ~200k rows. Should I use one of them instead of k-means so I don't have to pick k?
evals.expected_output: Warns that both Affinity Propagation and Mean Shift are O(n^2) in time/memory and will not scale to 200k rows; 'not choosing k' is misleading because both have parameters (preference, bandwidth) that implicitly control the cluster count. Redirects: if you genuinely don't want to pick k at this scale, use HDBSCAN (density params, scales better, handles noise) or MiniBatch k-means with a principled k-selection. Notes that no method is truly parameter-free. May note AP tends to produce many clusters and Mean Shift's niche is low-dimensional / image data.
expectations: States that Affinity Propagation and Mean Shift are O(n^2) / do not scale and are unsuitable for ~200k rows
Explains that these methods are not truly free of choosing cluster count — preference/bandwidth implicitly set it
Redirects to a scalable alternative (HDBSCAN for the no-preset-k goal, or MiniBatch k-means)
Conveys that no clustering method is genuinely parameter-free
